entities.name: Cyrus the Great
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Cyrus II (‘the Great,’ c. 600–530 BCE) was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire — the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean Sea to the Indus River — and the first ruler in history to articulate a policy of religious tolerance, human rights, and cultural autonomy for conquered peoples, as recorded in the Cyrus Cylinder (539 BCE), often called the ‘first declaration of human rights.’ Born to Cambyses I of Anshan and Mandane of Media, he united the Persian and Median tribes, overthrew his grandfather Astyages of Media (550 BCE), conquered the fabulously wealthy Lydian Empire of Croesus (546 BCE), and captured Babylon without significant resistance (539 BCE) by diverting the Euphrates River. His treatment of Babylon was revolutionary: rather than destroying the city and deporting its people (the Assyrian model), he restored temples, honored local gods, and freed captive peoples — including the Jews, whom he permitted to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple. For this act, the Hebrew Bible uniquely calls a non-Jewish king ‘messiah’ (anointed one, Isaiah 45:1). His empire’s administrative innovations — satrapies (provincial governorships), the Royal Road, a postal system, standardized weights and coinage, and the principle of governance by consent rather than mere terror — became the model for all subsequent Middle Eastern empires. Thomas Jefferson and the American Founding Fathers studied Xenophon’s Cyropaedia as a model of enlightened governance. The United Nations displayed a replica of the Cyrus Cylinder in 1971 as a symbol of human rights, and the Islamic Republic of Iran chose the Cyrus Cylinder’s winged disc as the emblem of Iran Air.
